body.text: NDIS participants critical of Quality and Safeguards Commission response to complaints
In short:
The regulator of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) is dealing with a significant backlog of just under 13,000 open complaints.
While the figure is an improvement on 15,000 open complaints in March, NDIS participants say serious complaints are going unaddressed for months.
A former senior staff member says the backlog is overwhelming the regulator and taking a toll on staff.

NDIS participants say serious reports of abuse, neglect and fraud are languishing for months, as data released by Freedom of Information reveals the regulator is grappling with a massive backlog of complaints.

In disturbing cases uncovered by the ABC, a participant with cerebral palsy had no support for three weeks after allegedly being defrauded of $16,000 from her plan, while in another case it took four months for a case worker to be assigned to look into reports of abuse and neglect.
A former senior NDIS Quality and Safety manager has told the ABC complaints are routinely closed without the regulator's staff having spoken to the person making the complaint.

Becki Greene, an NDIS participant who has multiple sclerosis and uses a wheelchair, first contacted the regulator, the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission, in May to complain about a provider who allegedly abused and neglected her.
The commission is tasked with investigating complaints against providers and disability workers, including allegations of abuse and harm, while working with other agencies to investigate fraud.
But Ms Greene said when she phoned, she was left on hold for an hour and 40 minutes, without ever getting through to a staff member.
"Having someone on hold for nearly two hours while they are distressed and distraught is completely unacceptable," she said of her experience.
When she tried to contact the commission again over the following days, she said she was left on hold for extended periods and was never able to speak to a staff member.
She then tried to submit an online complaint, but she said the commission's website timed her out midway.
Finally, she was able to lodge a complaint over email.

Despite repeated calls to the commission in which she was told it had been listed as a priority one case, it wasn't until the ABC made enquiries that a commission staff member phoned her, with a complaints officer only this week opening an investigation.
She said she was initially shocked by the long wait for a response to her complaint given its seriousness.
"I expected the commission to sit up and take notice," she said.
"It shouldn't have to take getting the media [involved] … for participants to be heard and have their complaint investigated."
The commission said it did not comment on individual cases but Acting Commissioner Natalie Wade explained that complaints were prioritised based on their urgency, seriousness and complexity.
"We use a risk-based prioritisation framework that helps us assess the level of risk and appropriate action," she said.
Ms Wade also said that the regulator remained "committed to continuous improvement and maintaining public confidence through meaningful and timely action on complaints and incidents".
Fraud complaint unaddressed after nine months
Disability advocate Elly Desmarchelier, who lives with autism and cerebral palsy, made a complaint to the commission over the previous Christmas/New Year period and still has not had any response.
Her complaint alleged that a former independent support worker claimed more than $16,000 in wages for shifts they did not work during the months after they had been let go.

When the support worker was contacted about the issue, they sent Ms Desmarchelier's plan manager an email where they said claims totalling $16,992 had been sent because of an "internal administrative error".
The worker offered to reimburse the money.
But Ms Desmarchelier said it was never repaid, meaning she lost that funding from her NDIS plan.
"I had three weeks where I did not have any support because I did not have funding to pay support workers," she said.

Ms Desmarchelier, a former National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) staff member who has been critical of the agency, made a complaint to both the commission and the NDIA's fraud team but hasn't heard back from either body.
Both agencies said they do not comment on individual cases.
She agreed the commission should prioritise complaints related to abuse or violence towards participants, where the risk to participants was highest.
But she said after such a long wait for a response to her complaint, she had now lost hope.
"I don't think I will ever get a response," Ms Desmarchelier said.
The disability advocate said she worried this created an environment where it was easier for people to do the wrong thing.
"If there is no threat of being held accountable, if you know you can get away with it, of course there is more opportunity to exploit disabled people,"
She said many in the disability community believed commission staff were doing the best they could but did not have enough resources.
"I have seen some good changes in the commission over the last few years but if you only have a certain amount of staff, there is only so much you can do," she said.
Complaints backlog shrinking, but concern still high
These experiences are not isolated.
Data released under Freedom of Information laws shows the commission had more than 15,000 open complaints as of March this year, down from a high of more than 25,000 open complaints in January 2025.
The commission told the ABC that figure had continued to drop and was now sitting at just under 13,000 open complaints.
That initial data was released by the commission to Mark Sweeney, a former senior NDIA executive who was with the public service for 20 years before being made redundant.
He took federal court action against the NDIA claiming he had been unfairly treated as a whistleblower, but that case was dismissed.

Mr Sweeney now publicly scrutinises the performance of the scheme and said the complaints backlog was still so large he believed it was overwhelming the regulator, even after its improvements in the past 18 months.

"I think what it probably indicates is that potentially they don't have enough staff — you know, their workflows are inefficient or they have a mismatch, an imbalance of staff monitoring the back of house as opposed to frontline workers," he said.
Mr Sweeney said the commission was also failing to meet its own target of closing half of the complaints within 90 days of being lodged.
"They've only achieved one in three complaint closures for the last two quarters," he said.
The former public servant said the commission's slow responses to many complaints created risks for NDIS participants.
"Participants could be in unsafe environments; participants could be getting ripped off," he explained.
Mr Sweeney has written to the Commonwealth Ombudsman requesting it investigate the systemic issues causing the complaints backlog, something Ms Greene said she also supported.
These latest allegations follow public criticism from disability workers in Western Australia's Kimberley region in July, who said the regulator had failed to act on serious complaints.
Ms Wade said the Commission had gone through significant organisational and regulatory reforms.

"The Commission continues to invest in its people, systems and processes to improve complaint handling and strengthen regulatory decision-making. As a result, the number of complaints awaiting action has reduced by 52 per cent since July 2025."
Cases allegedly closed without staff talking to complainants
A former senior manager at the commission spoke to the ABC about their experience working for the regulator.
They said the body's complaints team was understaffed right from its establishment in 2016 and "within three months of operating there was a backlog of complaints".

Speaking on the condition of anonymity because they feared reprisal, they said the issue had plagued the commission for the past decade and meant "important stuff took an incredibly long time to get to".
They said the size of the complaints backlog had "overwhelmed" the regulator and created an emotional toll for staff who cared about their work.
"If you are good at what you do and care about what you do, you are compromised the whole time you are there," they said.
"This has a devastating impact on overall morale and wellbeing."
The former staffer said complaints were routinely closed without a team member speaking to the person making the complaint.
The regulator's Acting Commissioner Natalie Wade defended the handling of complaints.
She said information from a range of sources was considered during complaint assessment, including written correspondence and online forms.
"Where additional information is required, or where it would assist the assessment, commission staff may contact the complainant directly," she said.
She said the regulator continued "to strengthen our compliance and enforcement efforts, improve complaint and incident management, and build a stronger regulatory intelligence capability".
